name: Ancient mound builders
summary: No music survives from Louisiana's mound-building cultures, and no instrument has been securely identified at Poverty Point. Archaeologists infer ceremony from plazas, platform mounds and feasting pits. The clearest hints of sound-making are pebble clusters in Marksville-era burials at the Crooks site, which were probably rattles, and a Caddo effigy pipe from Gahagan showing a frog holding a ceremonial rattle.

name: Native nations
summary: The songs and dances of Louisiana's Native nations are far older than the documented period that begins here, and they continue today. Caddo people keep the Turkey Dance and Drum Dance; Tunica-Biloxi singers have brought back songs in Tunica and Biloxi; Coushatta, Choctaw and Houma communities sing, drum and dance at home and at powwows. Many sacred songs, Chitimacha ones among them, are kept within the tribes.

name: Colonial French and Spanish
summary: European art and church music took root in New Orleans soon after its founding. In 1725 a Capuchin school opened and the parish church hired a musician and schoolmaster; the Ursuline nuns, who arrived in 1727, taught music and in 1754 received a manuscript of French and Italian works. The Theatre St. Pierre opened in 1792 and staged the city's first known opera in 1796.

name: Congo Square traditions
summary: The 1724 Code Noir made Sunday a day without work, and enslaved Africans gathered where they could to drum, sing and dance. An 1817 ordinance confined those gatherings to the square behind the city that became known as Congo Square, where the bamboula, calinda and other dances drew crowds until officials restricted and then suppressed them between the 1830s and 1850s. Their rhythms carried into second lines, Mardi Gras Indian music and jazz.

name: Creole and la-la
summary: French-speaking Black Creoles made their own music long before it was recorded; seven Louisiana Creole songs, a calinda among them, reached print in 1867. On the southwest prairies it became la-la, the fiddle and accordion music of house dances, alongside unaccompanied jure shouts, first recorded near Jennings in 1934. Amede Ardoin's recording sessions of 1929 to 1934 shaped both Creole and Cajun playing, and families such as the Carrieres of Lawtell and the Ardoins of Duralde carried la-la forward.

name: Cajun
summary: Acadian exiles who settled the Attakapas country and the Mississippi and Lafourche banks from 1765 brought French songs and fiddle dance tunes. Mixed with French Creole, Black Creole, Native and Spanish influences, these became recognizable Cajun music by the early twentieth century. First recorded in 1928, it lost ground to western swing before the accordion returned after World War II, and a wider revival followed the 1964 Newport Folk Festival.

name: Zydeco
summary: Zydeco grew in the late 1940s when Black Creole musicians in southwest Louisiana and the Texas oil towns added blues and rhythm and blues to la-la, driving it with accordion and the metal frottoir. Clarence Garlow's 1949 record Bon Ton Roula was an early marker, and Clifton Chenier, who signed with Specialty Records in 1955, defined the sound. Dance halls around Opelousas, Lawtell and Lafayette remain its home.

name: Jazz
summary: Jazz took shape in New Orleans when players such as cornetist Buddy Bolden, who formed his band in 1895, began improvising blues and quickening dance tunes, drawing on brass bands, ragtime and church music. Musicians carried it up the river and across the lake, and New Orleans bands were recorded from 1917. A revival beginning in the late 1930s led to Preservation Hall in 1961.

name: Brass band and second line
summary: Brass bands were everywhere in nineteenth-century New Orleans, and in the decades after Emancipation Black bands such as the Excelsior and Onward, prominent by the 1880s, played funerals, parades and dances. Benevolent societies and social aid and pleasure clubs hired them, and the dancing crowd that followed became the second line. The Dirty Dozen and Rebirth renewed the tradition in the 1980s.

name: Mardi Gras Indians
summary: Black New Orleanians have masked as Indians on Carnival day since at least the 1880s; Big Chief Tootie Montana traced the tradition to his great-uncle Becate Batiste, who founded the Creole Wild West around 1880. Their origins remain debated. The music is chant and song over percussion, first recorded commercially by Bo Dollis and the Wild Magnolias in 1971.
sources: 64 Parishes, Mardi Gras Indians <https://64parishes.org/entry/mardi-gras-indians> | 64 Parishes, Allison Tootie Montana <https://64parishes.org/entry/allison-tootie-montana>

name: Blues
summary: Blues emerged from work songs in the late nineteenth century, spreading as mail-order guitars became common in the 1890s. Lead Belly played Shreveport's Fannin Street as a teenager and was recorded at Angola in 1933. Rural players around Baton Rouge fed the laid-back swamp blues that Lightnin' Slim, Slim Harpo and others cut in Crowley from 1954, and Delta parishes kept an older country style.

name: Gospel and spirituals
summary: Black sacred song in Louisiana grew from antebellum spirituals and ring shouts, a lineage still visible in the Delta's Easter Rock, which participants remember as older than the Civil War. Jubilee and quartet singing followed, and New Orleans gave gospel Mahalia Jackson. White congregations in the Protestant north sang from shape-note books and at singing conventions, one of which drew about 10,000 people to Shreveport in 1937.

name: Country and the Hayride
summary: Country music grew from the ballads and fiddle tunes of Anglo-Celtic settlers in north Louisiana. The first Louisiana country record dates to 1925, and Shreveport's KWKH put string bands and Jimmie Davis on the air from 1928. From 1948 to 1960 the station's Louisiana Hayride, broadcast from Municipal Auditorium, launched Hank Williams, Elvis Presley and Johnny Cash and earned the name Cradle of the Stars.

name: R&B and early rock
summary: New Orleans rhythm and blues began with records cut at Cosimo Matassa's J&M studio, opened in 1947, where Roy Brown, Fats Domino, Lloyd Price and bandleader Dave Bartholomew built a rolling, horn-driven sound that fed directly into rock and roll. Between 1957 and 1961 Louisiana records placed about twenty-five singles a year on the national charts, before the British Invasion pushed the style aside.

name: Swamp pop
summary: Swamp pop appeared around 1955 when Cajun and Black Creole teenagers blended New Orleans rhythm and blues and early rock and roll with country and their own French music. It peaked between 1958 and 1964 with ballads such as Cookie and the Cupcakes' Mathilda, Rod Bernard's This Should Go On Forever and Phil Phillips's Sea of Love. Its home is Acadiana and neighboring southeast Texas, and its audience has since grown in the bayou and river parishes to the east.

name: Funk
summary: New Orleans funk is a rhythmically muscular descendant of the city's rhythm and blues. The Meters, formed in 1967 as Art Neville's pared-down band at the Ivanhoe on Bourbon Street, put ten singles on the rhythm and blues charts between 1969 and 1971 and helped define the genre while working as Allen Toussaint's studio band. They broke up in 1979, and rappers later sampled their grooves.
sources: 64 Parishes, The Meters <https://64parishes.org/entry/the-meters/> | 64 Parishes, Rhythm and Blues Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/rhythm-and-blues-music>

name: Bounce
summary: Bounce is New Orleans's own call-and-response party rap. It began in late 1991 when MC T. Tucker and DJ Irv recorded Where Dey At at the Ghost Town Lounge in Hollygrove, over the beat of the Showboys' Drag Rap. Local labels such as Take Fo' and Cash Money spread it through the 1990s, and Katey Red and Big Freedia later carried it to audiences worldwide.
sources: 64 Parishes, Bounce <https://64parishes.org/entry/bounce> | 64 Parishes, Rap, Hip-Hop, and Bounce Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/rap-hip-hop-and-bounce-music>

name: Hip-hop
summary: Rap took hold in New Orleans in the late 1980s, with the Ninja Crew's 1986 single among the first local records and Gregory D and Mannie Fresh close behind. Cash Money, founded in 1992, and Master P's No Limit made the city a national center of Southern rap by the late 1990s. Baton Rouge followed with Young Bleed, C-Loc, Boosie and Webbie, and later Kevin Gates.
sources: 64 Parishes, Rap, Hip-Hop, and Bounce Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/rap-hip-hop-and-bounce-music> | XXL, 12 Baton Rouge Rappers You Should Know <https://www.xxlmag.com/baton-rouge-rappers-you-should-know/>

name: Opera and concert music
summary: Opera reached New Orleans on May 22, 1796, with Grétry's Sylvain, and French-language companies at the Théâtre d'Orléans and, from 1859, the French Opera House made the city an opera capital. From the late 1830s to the 1850s English-speaking newcomers from the North added Protestant church music, amateur choral societies, sacred concerts, sheet music publishing and singing lessons in the new public schools. A symphony orchestra followed in 1936 and an opera association in 1943.

name: Marching bands
summary: Louisiana's school and college marching bands grew from military-style units into show bands. LSU's cadet band, organized in 1893, is the earliest documented here and was marching by about 1900. Southern's Human Jukebox built its name on playing current hits and meets Grambling's World Famed band each November at the Bayou Classic's Battle of the Bands, while New Orleans school bands fill Carnival parades and have trained many of the city's brass band musicians.
